<reason>PRO (Side B) won a competitive but clear debate by making the decision easier. Its central frame — that every CON fix (identity verification, bans, insured rides) is an operator duty, i.e., "more legal responsibility" with the label filed off — was never fully neutralized; CON's compliance-vs-fault distinction is legitimate but reads the motion narrowly as tort blame when it says "legal responsibility." PRO's pressure question on compensation forced CON into a per-ride insurance pool that the operator collects and administers, which PRO plausibly cast as concession. PRO also escaped the GPS-drift attack cleanly with the zone-wide speed cap, and its kinetic-energy closing dismantled CON's weak "changes speed, not aim" line. CON's best route — mode shift to cars — was real weighing that PRO handled poorly ("deflection," then "inconvenience"), but CON's chain from a half-block cap to district-wide throttling to more car deaths was speculative and overstated. CON also had two clipped turns and PRO one misreferenced ID pair, minor execution costs on each side. On balance PRO answered the sharpest pressure more directly and left the cleaner vote.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's second rebuttal/closing pivot from geofencing precision to a zone-wide speed cap, then the kinetic-energy point ("injuries are made of speed") against CON's "a throttle changes speed, not aim" — it turned CON's strongest technical objection into an argument that the operator holds a decisive, precision-free lever.</best_rebuttal>
